chunks.content: Interest in obesity has grown exponentially over the last years, with the availability of highly effective new pharmacological treatment options [ , ]. The increasing use of pharmacological treatment options has stimulated debates on several fundamental issues, including (1) full recognition of obesity as a disease, and more specifically a chronic, progressive relapsing one, as introduced by the World Health Organization [ ] and (2) optimization of the diagnostic criteria of obesity and the timing for offering different treatment options. Among other initiatives, the European Association for the Study of Obesity (EASO) has published documents on both diagnostic and treatment conceptual frameworks [ , ]. A large international group of > 50 experts has also been invited by the Lancet to discuss these topics, resulting in a comprehensive paper including guidance on obesity diagnostic assessment and treatment approaches [ ]. We aim at critically discussing here the similarities, discrepancies, and potential misunderstandings suggested by the EASO and Lancet Commission statements. Obesity diagnosis: BMI limitations Visceral fat in obesity diagnosis : Limitations of body mass index (BMI) in identifying not only obesity-associated clinical risk, but also different clinically relevant obesity phenotypes have been long acknowledged. WHO defines obesity as a disease characterized by excessive fat accumulation, which has been translated into the concept of “adiposity-based chronic disease” (ABCD) by the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists [ ] and the EASO [ ]. A high BMI is an invaluable tool to identify excess body mass as a proxy for excess body fat in clinical practice, and it remains a cornerstone for clinical obesity diagnosis and monitoring. However, BMI does not provide information on either fat amount or its distribution in the body and in the organs. Abdominal visceral fat accumulation can be detected using simple anthropometric surrogate measures based on waist circumference (WC) [ ], and all recent statements have strongly recommended the inclusion of WC, waist-to-hip, or waist-to-height in the diagnostic algorithm for obesity (LC). In particular, EASO focuses on waist-to-height ratio (EASO) with consideration of gender and ethnicity-specific cut-offs. The EASO statement has further proposed to consider elevated waist-to-height ratio as a diagnostic criterion for obesity also in the presence of BMI levels that were previously considered in the overweight range (BMI > 25 kg/m 2 ) [ ]. Similarly, the Lancet Commission defined WC-based measurements as “body size measurements” and proposed to confirm obesity diagnosis in the presence of at least two out of three altered parameters, regardless of elevated BMI [ ]. Thus, both statements move towards increasing consideration for abdominal visceral fat in obesity diagnosis, based on its predictive role for elevated health risk and complications [ , ]. These combined messages should hopefully strengthen awareness on the fundamental role of abdominal visceral fat in the pathophysiology and clinical history of obesity. Body composition (beyond body fat) :While the importance of abdominal visceral fat has been long recognized, the general concept of altered body composition and its profound clinical impact in persons with obesity is less appreciated, and they remain under-discussed in the EASO and Lancet Commission statements. The Lancet Commission included elevated body fat as an independent diagnostic criterion, and indeed sufficient for diagnosing obesity; although, no threshold for diagnosis was provided. It should also be pointed out that excess fat accumulation, per se, is inherently coupled to relative or absolute reductions in non-fat body compartments [ ] that may pose independent clinical challenges. Low muscle mass relative to total body weight, coupled with low muscle strength, has been recently introduced as a diagnostic criterion for sarcopenic obesity, and its negative clinical impact has been confirmed in recent years [ , ]. While an in-depth discussion of sarcopenic obesity is beyond the goals of the current paper, comprehensive assessment of body composition in clinical practice should be an important and timely discussion point for advocacy in the obesity community. This is all the more relevant at a time of rapid development in therapeutics for obesity management, with the introduction of obesity medications that likely have a profound impact on body composition [ , ] and whose risk–benefit assessment should become part of routine evaluation when the risk of substantial muscle loss is elevated [ ]. The EASO statement indeed supports the assessment of both muscle parameters and sarcopenic obesity, particularly among older adults [ ]. Besides and beyond more accurate measurement of excess body fat and its distribution, we strongly advocate for further implementation of body composition assessment in clinical practice, with priority for all patient groups at higher risk for loss of muscle mass and function [ ], using available techniques such as bioimpedance analysis (BIA) or dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA). Obesity as a disease—clinical impact and treatment complications Why obesity is a disease : obesity has been recognized as a chronic disease by clinicians and policymakers in a number of statements and settings [ – ]. However, this concept is not yet accepted in public awareness. Most importantly, patients and, to some extent, healthcare professionals, particularly those not involved in obesity care, still more or less openly fail to coherently embrace the concept that obesity is a chronic, progressive, and relapsing disease. On the contrary, obesity is unfortunately often considered a condition resulting from wrong choices and personal responsibilities in adopting “wrong” obesogenic lifestyles and not having the willingness or the strength to modify them. This judgemental approach is wrong and dangerous, leading to the obesity stigma that affects not only patients living with obesity but also the whole field of obesity, making allocation of resources for effective treatment extremely difficult. The body dissatisfaction and the obesity stigma favour thinness and criticize fat bodies, leading to “fatphobia” and the spread of eating disorders [ ]. We only wish to summarize below the main reasons why obesity fulfils all criteria for the definition of chronic disease, within the most accepted WHO-endorsed bio-psycho-social model, requiring biomedical, psychological, and social components. Further details are provided in recent reviews [ , ]. In summary: Biomedical component : biological mechanisms regulating energy balance, including appetite regulation and energy expenditure, are altered in obesity in pre-clinical and clinical studies [ ]. For instance, derangements include inefficient homeostatic and reward-associated components of appetite regulation, and altered energy expenditure through lipid oxidation and thermogenesis [ , ]. Also relevant, excess adipose tissue may also undergo maladaptive changes and fibrosis that make it a source of systemic inflammation with further negative impact on appetite regulation, reflecting the ABCD model [ ] with a strong pathogenetic role in the development of cardio-metabolic and other systemic complications [ ]. Psychological component : multiple psychological disorders contribute to the onset and complications of obesity. Data from the literature suggest a high prevalence of feeding and eating disorders in subjects with obesity: up to 79% present binge-eating symptoms and up to 25% night eating syndrome in the different studies [ ]. Beyond impaired reward mechanisms and their direct contribution to positive energy balance, a subgroup of patients demonstrates impulsive/compulsive eating behaviours (binge eating). These primary components also play a role in the commonly observed development of anxiety and depressive symptoms, with altered response to stress, which leads to further behavioural modifications. Social component : obesity is strongly influenced by socioeconomic and environmental factors in many ways. High food availability, lower food quality, and substantially reduced opportunities for physical activity and exercise are the main components of the obesogenic environment, which have interacted with biological and exposome-based factors, allowing the development of the ongoing global obesity epidemic. Social inequalities (e.g. disparities in access to health care and job opportunities) also exist in exposure to the risk of developing obesity, with lower socio-cultural level representing a strong risk factor worldwide. Exposome component : according to the exposome hypothesis, obesity arises from the complex interplay between genetic predisposition and the sum of all environmental exposures (such as diet, social environment, chemicals, stress, infections, and other external and internal factors) throughout a person’s life. This hypothesis highlights that obesity not only results from lifestyle or genetics alone, but also from the cumulative lifelong influence of a wide range of exposures [ ]. We therefore maintain that obesity must be considered a chronic disease (which needs long-term monitoring with a systemic approach), defined by altered body composition through excess body fat accumulation [ ]. Most importantly, in a large proportion of affected individuals, the onset of the disease is associated with stigma-associated distress and suffering, psychological distress, reduced quality of life, gradual limitations in routine activities as well as triggering of adiposity-based metabolic derangements that lead to systemic complications. Obesity, conversely, represents a major risk factor for a number of systemic complications, including all major non-communicable diseases as well as their acute complications, frailty, disabilities, and mental diseases. Lancet commission proposal: pre-clinical and clinical obesity : the Lancet Commission document [ ] has proposed a new classification into pre-clinical and clinical obesity. Interestingly, clinical obesity was defined as “a chronic disease …. characterised by signs and symptoms of ongoing organ dysfunction and/or reduced ability to conduct daily activities”, with a list of specific criteria to define organ dysfunction and autonomy levels that generally require the presence of symptomatic complications. On the other hand, pre-clinical obesity was defined as a “condition of excess body fat associated with variable level of health risk, but no ongoing illness” which “does not represent a disease diagnosis per se”. Importantly, pre-clinical obesity is not therefore proposed to represent an early disease stage, in the general absence of a staging framework. – Implications for obesity treatment : somewhat consistent with the above concepts, the Lancet Commission proposal recommends differential approaches for managing pre-clinical and clinical obesity. For the latter, focusing on “improvement or reversal of organ dysfunction” is recommended, as assessed by improvement of signs and symptoms rather than measures of weight loss. It is said that “people should have access to comprehensive care and evidence-based treatments to induce improvement (or remission when possible) of clinical manifestations of obesity and to prevent progression to end-organ damage developing clinical obesity as well as several other non-communicable diseases (NCDs), including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, certain types of cancer and mental illness, among others”. For pre-clinical obesity, focusing on risk reduction and prevention of progression is recommended through health counselling for weight loss or prevention of weight gain, and monitoring over time. It should be also pointed out that “level of care and type of intervention …. should be based on individual risk/benefit assessment, considering the severity of excess/abnormal adiposity and the presence/absence of other risk factors”. The overall approach proposed by the Lancet Commission raises the following concerns (Table ): It denies the defining obesity derangement (excess fat accumulation) as a disease in its own right; this indeed denies the above-mentioned criteria for disease definition and poses a high risk of perpetuating the obesity stigma for patients as well as a lack of resources for obesity management at large. It does not consider that comprehensive lifestyle interventions are effective only for a limited number of persons with obesity, suggesting that the patient is responsible for the prevention of “clinical obesity” [ – ]. This amplifies the bias and stigma against persons with obesity who should be able to manage obesity with lifestyle approaches (somehow going back to 'eat less, move more'). It separates the disease from its complications, indeed defining the disease a “condition” until complications are clinically evident. This concept is at odds with a number of diseases where a continuum is accepted between the onset of the defining derangement and progressive development of complications (e.g. diabetes, hypertension, organ failures). No one would dispute the need to treat diabetes without waiting for complications to arise. It appears to limit the concept of active early treatment for prevention of disease progression and complications by indicating health counselling as the primary intervention for pre-clinical obesity management. Early treatment has been long recognized as a priority for diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, or any other disease whose defining derangement (high blood glucose, high blood pressure, low haemoglobin) can be completely asymptomatic but is nevertheless actively managed in order to prevent complications or organ damage in the mid- to long-term. In obesity, limiting the concept of early treatment and prevention of complications is particularly alarming for children and adolescents that are exposed to a longer duration of fat accumulation and may experience earlier onset of life-threatening complications. Clinically advanced conditions are explicitly listed for the diagnosis of clinical obesity, such as the presence of NAFLD with liver fibrosis, obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome, or fatigue and lower limb oedema for heart failure. Such manifestations are characterized by poorer prognosis and could be prevented by actively managing obesity in earlier, “pre-clinical” stages. Clinical assessment was not described in detail, although references were provided to different available guidelines and guidance documents. Obesity staging : the same framework provided a conceptual recommendation that obesity be staged after diagnosis based on the presence and severity of its clinical component. The validity of the staging criterion, although the result of a consensus of experts from EASO, is currently being verified. In fact, different approaches for the staging of obesity, based on phenotyping and pathophysiology [ ], on the combination of organic, mental, and functional aspects [ ], considering the severity of the disease [ ], may be proposed to define a different combination/intensity of interventions. Considering obesity as a continuum, with different stages of severity, better approximates the similar context of other metabolic diseases than considering it in mutually exclusive preclinical/clinical categories. Management : a multimodal approach for obesity management was proposed, with comments on limited data availability on pharmacological and surgical treatment beyond BMI-based categories. In the context of a comprehensive clinical evaluation and with strong clinical emphasis on abdominal fat excess, the paper advocated for more research and clinical trials for pharmacological treatment focusing on these components. Targets for obesity management should emphasize improvement of its clinical component, beyond weight management. The framework on pharmacological treatment of obesity [ ] further reinforced this concept, while further emphasizing the indication for pharmacological treatment for weight management in the absence of complications, stating “total weight loss remains an important primary goal of treatment to reduce the risk of incident complications”. Conclusions Rapid evolution in obesity management opportunities has stimulated debate not only on optimization of obesity treatment, but also on its diagnostic components and its nature as a chronic disease leading to potentially fatal systemic complications. The EASO and Lancet Commission statements provide relevant contributions to this discussion. Expanding diagnosis to integrate abdominal visceral fat surrogates is not controversial, although consensus on anthropometric surrogates for abdominal visceral fat and their integration with altered BMI levels is still lacking. There is also emerging agreement on the need to integrate obesity complications and clinical domains beyond excess body fat accumulation, although proposed algorithms present significant conceptual differences. Perhaps unexpectedly, the Lancet Commission document has raised uncertainties and could cause potential confusion on the well-established nature of obesity as a chronic disease defined by pathological fat accumulation PER SE, independent of the presence of clinical complications. As discussed above, the proposal of pre-clinical obesity as an entity where excess fat is (1) not considered a disease per se and (2) is not considered a relevant health problem in the absence of advanced, clinically relevant complications raises significant concerns. This conceptual framework has the potential to lead to major setbacks in the fight against obesity stigma, the call for adequate resourcing to manage obesity, in reinforcing the need for early treatment of excess fat accumulation, to prevent complications, but also for immediate relief of its independent negative impact on health and health status. On a positive note, the Lancet Commission stated that “for some people with pre-clinical obesity and higher overall health risk, other interventions (pharmacological or surgical) might be warranted, proportional to the level of risk and the presence of other conditions that could benefit from reduction of weight or adiposity”. chunks.content: Introduction Acromegaly is a rare but significant endocrine disorder typically caused by a growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma. The disease manifests with progressive physical changes such as enlarged hands, feet, and coarse facial features, and is often associated with comorbidities such as cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, hypertension, and joint disorders ( ). Timely and effective diagnosis and management of acromegaly is crucial to prevent complications, and it typically involves a combination of surgery, pharmacotherapy (e.g., somatostatin analogs, growth hormone receptor antagonists, and dopamine agonists), and occasionally radiotherapy ( , ). Pituitary surgery, especially via the transsphenoidal approach, is a key method for achieving biochemical remission in treating pituitary adenomas. If surgery is unsuccessful or not an option, medical treatments are considered ( ). First-generation somatostatin analogs (SSA) are widely used as first line medical option and provide adequate disease control in 30-50% of cases, with some patients experiencing adenoma shrinkage ( ). Pegvisomant, a growth hormone (GH) receptor antagonist, is used when first-generation SSAs are not enough to control the disease ( ). Pasireotide long-acting release (LAR), a second-generation SSA, can be effective in those who do not respond to first-generation SSAs but may cause significant hyperglycemia ( ). Dopamine agonists are moderately effective and are used primarily in mild cases or as add on in a combination therapy ( ). Focused radiotherapy is a last resort for patients who are not controlled after surgery and/or medical therapy ( ). Optimal treatment can be challenging in areas with limited healthcare resources, which is often the case in many regions, including the Arabian Gulf region. In the Gulf region, the treatment of acromegaly varies considerably due to differences in healthcare infrastructure, availability of specialized care, health insurance coverage and access to new medical therapies ( , ). Moreover, the availability of advanced surgical interventions and radiotherapy can vary, with some countries facing limitations in access to these services, which may delay optimal treatment and outcomes. Given these challenges, there is an urgent need for regional guidelines and consensus for the management of acromegaly within the Gulf region. Such guidelines would help standardize treatment practices, ensure consistency in clinical decision-making, and allow healthcare providers to deliver the most effective care within available resource constraints. Consensus-driven regional guidelines, based on local resources and healthcare needs, would also improve early diagnosis and treatment, thereby preventing the long-term complications of acromegaly. Moreover, such guidelines could help minimize the variations in practice across the region, ensuring that all patients, regardless of country, receive equitable and evidence-based care. A working group of 15 experts from 6 Gulf countries was convened and the Delphi survey technique ( ) was employed to develop appropriate guidelines and reach a consensus on the management of acromegaly in the Gulf region, considering the available healthcare resources and the challenges faced by these different countries. The goal is to provide evidence-based recommendations tailored to the specific healthcare settings of the region, ensuring standardized care while addressing variations in treatment access, availability of resources, and regional expertise. Methodology The Delphi method To achieve this objective, the Delphi methodology was utilized to gather expert opinions and reach consensus on key aspects of acromegaly management. The Delphi method is a structured, iterative process involving a panel of experts who anonymously provide their opinions and recommendations on specific questions. This process allows for the development of evidence-based guidelines while considering the nuances of local healthcare conditions and resources. This study followed the DELPHISTAR reporting guidelines for Delphi studies, and the completed checklist is included as . Participant selection A scientific committee of five expert endocrinologists (MA, TE, KA, MM, AE) developed the study objectives and designed an online survey focusing on the treatment and follow-up of acromegaly. A panel of 15 experts in acromegaly management was selected based on their qualifications and clinical experience, representing all six Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries (Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, and Oman). This geographically diverse panel was assembled to ensure comprehensive coverage of regional endocrine practices. While the panel size (n=15) may appear limited, expertise and regional representation were prioritized over quantity, in alignment with Delphi methodology standards for rare diseases. Furthermore, endocrinologist with focused practice in acromegaly are limited in the region. These 15 participants are known for their expertise in acromegaly care and represent the majority of the available experts in the Gulf region. All panelists were senior endocrinologists with at least ≥5 years of acromegaly management experience, ensuring depth of insight and clinical relevance. The final questionnaire spanned six domains: primary treatment, pre-surgical SSA use, second-line therapies, radiotherapy, post-surgical follow-up, and long-term monitoring. Each statement in the questionnaire was rated on a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from strong agreement to strong disagreement. This enabled experts to share their insights and highlight key challenges in managing acromegaly, considering current practices, local healthcare resource constraints, and available treatment options in their country. The questionnaire was accessible through an online platform (Google Forms), and responses were collected anonymously. Consensus was defined as 66.8% or more panelists rating their agreement as either “agree” or “disagree” on the Likert scale ( ). After the first round of responses, the scientific committee reviewed the feedback. Statements that did not reach the consensus threshold were revised for clarity, leading to the rephrasing of 10 statements and the removal of 3. These revisions were then resubmitted for further review in a second round on the same platform. The second round of the online Delphi survey included 10 statements from the first round. Panel members were encouraged to reconsider their initial responses considering group feedback to achieve consensus. After this round, the scientific committee reviewed the feedback. Three statements that still did not reach the consensus threshold were revised, necessitating a third and final round conducted as a virtual meeting. This meeting focused on the three statements that failed to achieve consensus in the second round, resulting in the rephrasing of two statements and the removal of one, thereby reaching the consensus threshold. The complete questionnaire, along with the consolidated responses, was sent to the entire group to represent the majority opinion, allowing experts to provide their final approval or suggestions for further refinement of the consensus. . Data analysis Predefined criteria were established to determine the conditions under which the conclusions of the Delphi study would be considered reached. Consensus was defined as having been reached when a minimum agreement threshold of 66.8% was met ( ). There was a strong consensus on referring patients with acromegaly to specialized centers with both medical and surgical expertise (93.8% agreement). Surgical intervention was overwhelmingly supported, with 100% agreement that surgery should be the preferred first-choice treatment for all eligible patients with acceptable surgical risk. Furthermore, consensus was reached that surgery remains the first-choice treatment for growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenomas both with (100% agreement) and without visual pathway compression (87.5% agreement). Moreover, 68.8% of the panelists disagreed with considering somatostatin analogues (SSA) as the first-choice treatment instead of surgery for invasive macroadenomas lacking visual pathway compression. Pre-surgery treatment with SSAs was supported by 75.0% of the panelists to be used when the surgery is delayed, and 93.8% agreed that SSAs reduce surgical and anesthesia-related risks in patients with high surgical risk such as patients with severe pharyngeal thickening, sleep apnea, or high-output heart failure. Nonetheless, there was 75% agreement against routine pre-surgical SSAs treatment due to insufficient evidence for improved outcomes. In the realm of second-line treatment, 93.8% supported watchful waiting for asymptomatic patients with marginally elevated insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) levels, and 100% agreed on initiating first-generation SSAs treatment for symptomatic patients with elevated IGF-1 post-surgery. Repeat surgery was unanimously endorsed for symptomatic patients with potentially resectable tumor remnants, while 81.3% acknowledged biochemical resistance to first-generation SSAs under specific conditions, and 93.7% agreed on recognizing radiological resistance according to defined parameters. Notably, there was substantial support (100%) for utilizing combination therapy where resources are available, notably SSAs with pegvisomant or cabergoline for patients failing to achieve IGF-1 normalization. Regarding radiotherapy, there was a 100% consensus regarding its role as a second-line treatment post-surgery for symptomatic patients with unresectable tumors and as a fallback for those unable to afford medical therapy. On the contrary, there was a 75.1% disagreement on using radiotherapy as a first-line treatment for

Regarding radiotherapy, there was a 100% consensus regarding its role as a second-line treatment post-surgery for symptomatic patients with unresectable tumors and as a fallback for those unable to afford medical therapy. On the contrary, there was a 75.1% disagreement on using radiotherapy as a first-line treatment for symptomatic patients with invasive adenomas. In terms of post-surgical follow-up, experts unanimously recommended initiating the first clinical and biochemical evaluation within 1–3 months after surgery, alongside a 100% agreement on defining disease remission when post-surgery random GH levels are undetectable and accompanied by normal IGF-1 levels. There was also 93.7% consensus on adjusting SSAs dosages after the third injection based on the patient’s biochemical response. Regarding long-term follow-up, 100% of panelists supported lifelong monitoring for patients on medical treatment, while significant disagreement (68.8%) arose concerning follow-up for patients controlled by surgery alone who do not require treatment for pituitary insufficiency. Overall, these findings reflect a robust inclination toward surgical intervention as the primary treatment for acromegaly, emphasizing the importance of specialized care and long-term patient follow-up. Discussion Acromegaly is a rare but serious disorder, often associated with diagnostic delays and suboptimal treatment outcomes, especially in regions with limited access to specialized care ( ). In the Gulf region, disparities in healthcare resources and expertise necessitate the establishment of region-specific guidelines to harmonize care and optimize outcomes. Prior studies have emphasized the variability in acromegaly management globally, with differences in access to advanced medical therapies such as first and second generation SSAs and pegvisomant ( , ). This study bridges this gap by incorporating expert opinions from across the GCC countries, ensuring that recommendations are feasible and relevant to the region. The findings from the Delphi consensus process provide critical insights into the management of acromegaly in the gulf region, emphasizing the need for a multifaceted and evidence-based approach. All experts (100%) agreed that surgery should be the primary treatment for eligible patients. This aligns with previous research suggesting that surgical resection of growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenomas is often the most effective means of achieving long-term disease control and improving patient outcomes ( , ). Recent studies reinforce the notion that surgery should remain the first-line intervention for symptomatic acromegaly, particularly when dealing with tumors amenable to resection. The expert consensus also highlighted the complexities surrounding the use of SSAs in different clinical scenarios. While 93.8% of panelists supported utilizing SSAs pre-surgery to mitigate surgical and anesthesia-related risks in high-risk individuals, there was a notable disagreement (68.8%) regarding the use of SSAs as a first-line treatment compared to surgical intervention for invasive macroadenomas. This reflects a similar trend reported in the literature, where the preference for surgical management is evident when complete resection is anticipated ( ). Melmed (2018) emphasizes that while SSAs are valuable as second-line therapies or adjuncts, they are generally not recommended as substitutes for surgery, particularly in cases where surgical intervention is feasible ( ). The consensus also underscores the importance of pre-surgical and post-surgical management strategies. The agreement from 75.1% of panelists on the importance of SSAs as an interim treatment when surgery is delayed complements findings from recent studies that advocate for optimized care continuity even when immediate surgical intervention is not possible ( , ). However, the consensus against routine pre-surgical SSA use due to insufficient evidence for improved outcomes mirrors caution expressed in prior evaluations ( – ). When discussing second-line treatment protocols, the expert panel reached a 93.8% consensus in favor of watchful waiting for asymptomatic patients with marginally elevated IGF-1 levels (1.5–2× the upper limit of normal [ULN]) during the early post-operative period (3–6 months). This cautious approach aligns with current guidelines advocating against overtreatment in borderline cases ( ). The 1.5–2× ULN threshold was specifically adopted from the ACROPRAXIS program Delphi survey—a study on acromegaly management in clinical practice settings in Spain—which underscores the necessity of individualized decision-making in clinically ambiguous scenarios ( ). The panel agreed that radiological resistance is defined as an increase in tumor size or < 20% tumor shrinkage on MRI from baseline after receiving the maximum tolerated dose of SSA therapy for 6–12 months. This definition is consistent with what was proposed by Colao et al. ( ). Patients meeting this criterion are usually less likely to achieve biochemical control with first-generation SSA alone. Therefore, consideration of add-on therapy to SSA (e.g., pegvisomant) or changing from first-generation SSA to pasireotide is an option. This definition is consistent with what was proposed by Colao et al. ( ). Patients meeting this criterion are usually less likely to achieve biochemical control with first-generation SSA alone. Therefore, consideration of add-on therapy to SSA (e.g., pegvisomant) or changing from first-generation SSA to pasireotide is an option. The acknowledgment of biochemical and radiological resistance to SSAs reflects a refined understanding of heterogeneous treatment responses. This approach aligns with the Pituitary Society’s updated recommendations on acromegaly management, which stress the importance of vigilant monitoring and timely therapeutic adjustments in resistant cases ( ). Medical therapy for acromegaly can be personalized based on patient characteristics and biomarkers to improve treatment outcomes. For example, patients with T 2 MRI hyperintensity and specific receptor expressions (low SST2, high SST5) show better responses to pasireotide, while combination therapy with low-dose SSAs and weekly pegvisomant offers both effectiveness and cost benefits ( ). Some experts consider that pasireotide can be used as first-line therapy in patients with specific characteristics, including T 2 MRI hyperintensity, receptor expression patterns, and certain immunohistochemical patterns ( ). Lim and Fleseriu (2022) further emphasized that factors such as sparsely granulated adenomas, low SSTR2 status, and genetic mutations can predict resistance to first-generation SSAs, suggesting these patients might be better candidates for pegvisomant or pasireotide treatment ( ). In the context of radiotherapy, the unanimous support for its role as a second-line treatment coincides with established literature advocating for radiotherapy in patients who do not respond adequately to surgical or medical treatments ( ). This suggests that while surgery remains critical, radiotherapy plays a supportive role when other options are untenable. The panel’s disagreement regarding radiotherapy as a first-line treatment for invasive adenomas reinforces the prevailing view that surgical options should be prioritized when feasible even if the surgery will be for debulking rather than cure ( ). The expert consensus further emphasizes the necessity of structured post-operative follow-up, with unanimous support for initial biochemical evaluations within 1–3 months post-surgery. This is consistent with recent recommendations suggesting that early assessment of treatment effectiveness is crucial for guiding subsequent management and ensuring patient safety ( , ). Additionally, defining remission based on undetectable GH levels alongside normal IGF-1 levels reflects a consensus that mirrors findings by Melmed S et al. ( ), who established similar criteria for treatment success. Finally, consensus on the need for lifelong follow-up for patients on medical treatment—while seeing significant disagreement on long-term monitoring for those managed and cured solely through surgery—highlights an area requiring further research to optimize follow-up strategies. This Delphi consensus provides a comprehensive overview of expert opinions on acromegaly management, advocating for surgical intervention as the cornerstone of treatment while acknowledging the valuable role of adjunctive therapies. These results contribute to an evolving understanding of acromegaly management and underscore the need for tailored, patient-centered approaches in clinical practice. While this study represents an important step toward standardizing acromegaly management in the Gulf region, it has limitations. The reliance on expert opinion may introduce bias, and the findings may not fully capture the diversity of practices across all GCC countries. Additionally, the lack of robust local data on acromegaly epidemiology and treatment outcomes highlights the need for future research to validate these recommendations in regional practice. Conclusion These Delphi consensus findings provide a comprehensive synthesis of expert opinions on the management of acromegaly, highlighting the key role of surgical intervention while recognizing the importance of medical adjuncts. As the field continues to evolve, these insights reinforce the necessity for ongoing research and collaboration among clinicians to refine treatment approaches, improve patient outcomes, and tailor management strategies to individual patient circumstances.

chunks.content: Introduction Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) constitute the major cause of death in developed countries, representing 32% of annual deaths worldwide and involve high economic costs for public health systems (Available from, ). High low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDLc) plasma levels are associated with CVDs (Cholesterol-lowering bioactive foods & nutraceuticals in pediatrics: clinical evidence of efficacy & safety., ). Childhood is the optimal period for early hypercholesterolemia screening, since although cardiovascular events are not common in children, they may have morphological and functional modifications in the vessel wall, since the atherosclerotic process can start very early in life (Kusters Dorothé et al., ). Hypercholesterolemia is usually countered by a healthy lifestyle (diet and physical activity) and cholesterol-lowering medications that prevent eventual clinical complications associated with these diseases (Ademi et al., ). Due to the long-term efficacy and adverse events of pharmacological interventions, public health programs claim the importance of adopting healthy diets and lifestyle habits, mainly in children and young adults, committed to the improvement of plasma lipid profile, intending to delay pharmacological interventions and the onset of clinical complications (Kaminsky et al., ). Among different CVD-preventing interventions, a wide range of clinical trials highlight the effectiveness of the Mediterranean diet as a traditional balanced diet and lifestyle habits, in which extra-virgin olive oil (EVOO) plays a key role as the main culinary fat (Martínez-González et al., ). The health-enhancing properties of EVOO are attributed to the presence of several constituents, including unsaturated fatty acids, mostly represented by oleic acid, and other minor phytochemical constituents, such as polyphenols i.e., tyrosols, oleuropein, and other secoiridoids; tocopherols; triterpenoid acids, such as maslinic and oleanoic acids; and phytosterols such as campesterol, β-sitosterol, fucosterol, and stigmasterol (Paz et al., ). Phytosterols are considered efficient plant-derived hypocholesterolemic agents because of their structural similarity to cholesterol, which interferes with their absorption, biosynthesis, and metabolism in the human body. Therefore, they have recently been considered promising candidates for the treatment of hypercholesterolemia and associated complications in children (Wójcik, ). Lipidomics has emerged as a powerful tool to comprehensively characterize lipid profiles and to elucidate their roles in health and disease. In this framework, phytosterols are of particular interest, as their structural similarity to cholesterol allows them to modulate lipid metabolism and influence membrane dynamics. Integrating phytosterol research into lipidomics not only provides a deeper understanding of their biological functions but also opens avenues for identifying novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets related to metabolic disorders, cardiovascular health, and nutrition. The present interventional, crossover, clinical trial aimed to evaluate the effect of the daily intake of a spreadable cream based on EVOO enriched in phytosterols (PESC) for 8 weeks on children and adolescents with untreated hypercholesterolemia compared with the intake of a control EVOO-spreadable cream without phytosterols (CSC). Anthropometric and biochemical parameters related to cardiovascular risk and a lipidomics-based workflow, via liquid chromatography coupled with high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-HRMS), were performed to decipher the effect of PESC administration at a lipid metabolome-wide level. Chemometric analyses and the application of multivariate statistics-based chemometric tests were used to better interpret the particular effects of either single or combined factors on the plasma lipid profile of children with hypercholesterolemia. Our data opens new perspectives for the management of hypercholesterolemia and paves the way for the design of novel functional food products. Methods Extra virgin olive oil-based phytosterols-enriched spreadable cream and control spreadable cream The PESC experimental spreadable cream, based on EVOO and enriched in phytosterols, and the CSC control cream were prepared in 15 g single-dose containers using a base of 90% EVOO. Each single dose of PESC preparation was added with 1.2 g of free phytosterols (Vegapure 95E, Reference: 30,534,530, CAS: 83-48-7, BASF Nutrition & Health, Germany), whereas the CSC was the same EVOO-spreadable cream without phytosterols. The experimental dose of phytosterols was adjusted in compliance with the European regulation 2000/500/CE, which sets a maximum daily amount of 3 g/day of free plant sterols, which represents 8% of free phytosterols in the experimental spreadable cream. The EVOO-spreadable creams were prepared in ACER CAMPESTRES S.L. Table shows the chemical compositions of the two spreadable creams. Phytosterols were analyzed using gas chromatography at the Instituto de la Grasa (CSIC, Sevilla), as previously described (García-González et al., ). Considering an average weight of approximately 20 kg for 6-year-old children, 40 kg for 12-year-old and 60 kg for 16-year-old, the doses of plant sterols were adjusted for weight ranges. Children weighing > 20 kg and < 40 kg received a single daily 15-g dose of spreadable cream (0.03–0.06 g plant sterols/kg of body weight/day), whereas children weighing ≥ 40 kg and up to 60 kg received two 15-g doses per day (0.04–0.06 g plant sterols/kg of body weight/day). Since both PESC and CSC were EVOO-based, participation in this study did not entail any potential risks. Experimental design A

Experimental design A randomized, double-blind, crossover, controlled trial was conducted in the Reina Sofía University Hospital of Córdoba (Spain), comprising the daily consumption of PESC compared with the control CSC creams. The intervention was conducted for 5 months divided into two periods of 8 weeks separated by a wash-out period of 4 weeks, after which crossover was carried out. Allocation into the two sequences of spread cream administration was performed using a stratified block randomization method adjusted for age and sex. The randomization list was concealed in a light-proof sealed envelope. The sealed envelope was maintained by an independent statistician. Therefore, the children and researchers were blinded to treatment allocation throughout the study. Blood pressure, body mass index, and blood sampling were performed before and after the two 8-week intervention periods (t1 and t2). The participants were instructed to return the individual spreadable containers that were not consumed during each intervention period for compliance determination. Intervention compliance was calculated as a percentage by dividing the dosages consumed by those indicated for the entire period of intervention. The protocol was conducted following the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice Guidelines (Vijayananthan & Nawawi, ; World Medical Association, ). All investigators were qualified to conduct and supervise the trial. The parents or tutors of the participants provided written informed consent before study entry. The sample size was calculated assuming a decrease in total cholesterol of 10%, an alpha error of 0.05, a type-2 Beta error of 0.2, and a loss of children of 15% throughout the study, indicating 25 children for each group were required. The clinical trial protocol has been registered previously in: https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT05460208 . Participants and eligibility Fifty-six children and adolescents (33 boys and 23 girls) were recruited from the pediatric Clinical Management Unit of the Reina Sofía University Hospital in Córdoba (Spain). The inclusion criteria were as follows: children between 6 and 18 years old who agreed to participate in the study and whose parents were willing to provide written informed consent for adherence to the protocol, diagnosed with hypercholesterolemia, and not receiving any treatment for hypercholesterolemia or any other pathology. The exclusion criteria were as follows: intake of hypocholesterolemic drugs or any other drug, suffering from other metabolic diseases, and unwillingness to sign the informed consent. Six children did not meet the inclusion criteria, and only 50 children were finally included (30 boys and 20 girls). Children were randomly divided into two groups. Daily, children allocated to group A (n = 24; 13 boys and 11 girls) received the corresponding dose of the control CSC (depending on their body weight, as described above) for 8 weeks, whereas children in group B (n = 26; 17 boys and 9 girls) received the corresponding dose of the enriched PESC during the same period. Eight weeks after the administration of the spreadable cream, it was interrupted, and a wash-out period of 4 weeks was initiated. One boy and two girls from group A dropped out during the first period of intervention because they did not like the spread texture. Afterward, a crossover for both groups was implemented, and children in group A (n = 21; 12 boys and 9 girls) took the PESC cream, while those in group B (n = 26; 17 boys and 9 girls) took the CSC cream during the following 8 weeks. During the second intervention period, one boy from group B and three girls from group A dropped out because they did not want to be drawn again. Thus, only 18 children (12 boys and 6 girls) from Group A and 25 children (16 boys and 9 girls) from Group B remained in the study at the end of the intervention. Additionally, to find a reliable effect of phytosterol intake, we calculated adherence to the intervention compliance and for statistical data analysis we established a cut-off value to select those samples from subjects presenting at least 70% of treatment adherence. In addition, the MS tolerances for peak centroiding were 0.01 Da and 0.05 Da for MS/MS. The identification step (set > 50% for annotation) was based on mass accuracy, isotopic pattern, and spectral matching, considering the usual ion adducts for lipidomics. To fill in missing peaks, gap-filling based on the peak finder algorithm was used considering a 5-ppm tolerance for m/z values. To conclude, using an identification score > 5, in in-silico fragmentation of the not fully annotated MS/MS features was achieved using MS-Finder software, considering the available database (i.e., Lipid Maps). Chemometrics analyses, data processing and statistics The experimental design included three factors: group (A or B), treatment (PESC for the experimental group, and CSC for the control group), and sampling time (before and after the intervention, t1 and t2, respectively). Lipidomics results were thoroughly processed using different chemometric analyses. First, to determine the influence of each factor on the lipid profile of plasma samples, unsupervised hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA) was performed using Mass Profiler Professional software (Agilent Technologies®, Santa Clara, CA, USA), as previously described (El-Nakhel et al., ). For this purpose, the abundance of annotated features was subjected to log 2 transformation, normalization at the 75th percentile, and baselining against the median value of all samples. The resulting hierarchical cluster was obtained based on a fold-change-based heatmap and combined with a dendrogram built on Euclidean distances by applying the Ward’s linkage rule. Additionally, a supervised multivariate analysis based on the analysis of variance (ANOVA) multi-block orthogonal partial least squares (AMOPLS) was performed using the “rAMOPLS” package (version 0.2) in the R software (version 4.2.3), as previously described (Boccard et al., ). The identified VIP 2 markers included a large proportion (20%) of phospholipids and lysophospholipids, showing an accumulation of phospholipids for PESC at t2 (logFC = 0.20–1.58), with PE P-15:2/17:4 being significantly accumulated ( p < 0.05), whereas the lysophospholipid LPC 9:0 accumulated in CSC at t2 (logFC = −0.31). However, for severe hypercholesterolemia and familial hypercholesterolemia, it is necessary to combine dietary treatment with pharmacological treatment mainly statins (Turini et al., ). Pharmacotherapy in children and adolescents is only recommended from the age of 10 years when they do not respond positively to lifestyle modifications, particularly for those with LDLc serum levels ≥ 190 mg/dL (Jellinger et al., ). This fact is probably because the main mechanism of action of phytosterols is intestinal competition with cholesterol for micellization, transport, and absorption (Li et al., ), and they scarcely reach the bloodstream. Borel reported that the effectiveness of the absorption of sitosterol and campesterol is approximately 0.51–1.9% (Borel, ), and Li et al. agreed that the intestinal absorption rate of phytosterols is less than 5%, much lower than that of cholesterol (50–60%), and depends on many genetic, physiological, and nutritional factors (Li et al., ). In fact, some authors have suggested that the hypocholesterolemic effect of phytosterols may be mediated by changing the structure of the gastrointestinal microbiota (Lv et al., ). One limitation of the present study is that we have not analyzed microbiota changes induced by the intake of the phytosterol-enriched cream, nor metabolites derived from its metabolism. Therefore, more studies are needed to identify these potential microbiota-derived hypocholesterolemic mechanisms. Given the complexity of the lipid profile provided by the lipidomics approach, the application of multivariate chemometrics analyses is essential to determine the biological significance of annotated metabolites and to better interpret the effect of phytosterol intake on lipid metabolism modulation in the children included in the present study. Lipids corresponding to such classes were among the top metabolites in the Group x Treatment interaction (Table ). One of the main strengths of AMOPLS is that it has individual predictive components, each focused on a specific effect or interaction. As a result, regardless of the variability explained by each factor or the significance of other factors, it allows for the independent biological interpretation of each independent factor. Therefore, we extracted that the main discriminant metabolites associated with the interaction “Time x Treatment” were phospholipids and lysophospholipids (20%), sphingolipids (20%), as well as DAGs and VAEs. chunks.content: Introduction Hyperglycemia is the major factor responsible for diabetic microvascular complications, i.e. retinopathy, neuropathy, and nephropathy in T2DM ( – ) and progressive beta cell failure is the primary pathophysiologic abnormality responsible for the development and progression of hyperglycemia ( ). Chronic elevation in the plasma glucose concentration also contributes to the progressive decline in beta cell function, i.e. glucotoxicity ( ), creating a negative feedback cycle in which the defect in insulin secretion exacerbates the hyperglycemia. Studies in experimental animals and in man have demonstrated that chronic hyperglycemia impairs beta cell function ( – ) and, conversely, correction of the hyperglycemia improves beta cell function ( – ). The current therapeutic recommendation for patients with new onset diabetes, as well as those with long standing diabetes and very high HbA1c, e.g. >10%, is insulin therapy ( , ). Insulin can effectively lower the plasma glucose concentration independent of beta cell function, ameliorate the glucotoxic effect of hyperglycemia on the beta cell ( – ), and reduce the HbA1c to 6.5–7.0% ( , ). Based upon this rational, the ADA ( ) and AACE ( ) have recommended the institution of insulin therapy in T2DM patients with high HbA1c while switching to non-insulin therapy after removal of glucose toxicity (3–6 months). This recommendation is based upon consensus rather than evidence because patients with HbA1c >10% usually are excluded from clinical studies and very few studies have included T2DM patients with HbA1c >10%. The etiology of T2DM is complex and involves multiple metabolic disturbances collectively known as Ominous Octet ( ). Using cluster analysis, a recent study ( ) has demonstrated multiple metabolic phenotypes in newly diagnosed T2DM patients, e.g. T2DM patients with primarily insulin deficiency versus primarily insulin resistance. We previously ( ) have shown that in very poorly controlled T2DM patients (HbA1c >10%) with long standing disease (~10 years) residual beta cell function (measured with the increase from baseline to 120 minute [OGTT] in plasma C-peptide concentration [CPEP 120 /CPEP 0 ]) influences the response to antidiabetic therapy. Thus, only poorly controlled T2DM patients with depleted beta cell function (<56% increase in CPEP above baseline, i.e. CPEP 120 /CPEP 0 <1.56) required insulin therapy for glycemic control, while subjects with CPEP 120 /CPEP 0 >1.56 achieved the ADA HbA1c goal <7.0% using combination therapy with GLP-1 receptor agonist (RA) plus thiazolidinedione. Further, obese T2DM patients manifest severe insulin resistance which should be addressed in order to achieve optimal glycemic control ( ). Thus, including TZD in glucose lowering therapy, which is the only true insulin sensitizer available, will address both major core defects of T2DM, beta cell dysfunction and insulin resistance ( ). The EDICT study ( , ) compared the efficacy of two glucose lowering therapeutic strategies in newly diagnosed T2DM patients: (i) initiation of Triple Therapy with metformin plus pioglitazone plus GLP-1 RA at the time of diagnosis versus (ii) initiation of therapy with metformin followed by sequential addition of sulfonylurea followed by basal insulin to maintain the HbA1c at <6.5%. Because there was no upper limit for HbA1c inclusion, 104 study participants had an initial HbA1c >10% and all manifested weight loss in the preceding months. In the present study, we analyzed the response to therapy in patients with initial an HbA1c >10% to identify factors which predict the need for insulin therapy in newly diagnosed T2DM patients who presented with very high HbA1c. Research Design and Methods The EDICT study ( E fficacy and D urability of I nitial C ombination T herapy for Type 2 Diabetes) is an open-label, randomized controlled trial ( NCT01107717 ) designed to compare the efficacy and durability of two therapeutic approaches in newly diagnosed T2DM patients: (1) initial Triple Combination Therapy with metformin/pioglitazone/exenatide versus (2) initiating therapy with metformin followed by stepwise addition of glipizide and then glargine insulin upon failure to achieve the treatment target (Conventional Therapy). The study protocol was approved by Institutional Review Board of University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio and informed written consent was obtained from all participants before enrolment. The study design ( ) and primary outcome ( ) previously have been published. Briefly, drug naïve, new onset (<2 years) T2DM patients, age=18–75 years, who otherwise were healthy, were recruited into the study. Key exclusion criteria were: positive anti-GAD antibody, use of medications known to affect glucose metabolism, previous treatment with any antidiabetic agent, evidence of proliferative retinopathy, albumin excretion > 300 mg/day, or major organ system disease as determined by physical examination, medical history and screening blood tests. Drug naïve, newly diagnosed T2DM patients were consecutively randomized in the EDICT study to receive either initial Triple Therapy or Conventional Therapy to maintain HbA1c <6.5% (48 mmol/mol). A total of 318 participants were enrolled in EDICT study. The present study

Drug naïve, newly diagnosed T2DM patients were consecutively randomized in the EDICT study to receive either initial Triple Therapy or Conventional Therapy to maintain HbA1c <6.5% (48 mmol/mol). A total of 318 participants were enrolled in EDICT study. The present study is a post hoc analysis that included only EDICT participants with baseline HbA1c > 10.0% (n=104). Participants randomized to Triple Therapy were started simultaneously on metformin/pioglitazone/exenatide, while participants receiving Conventional Therapy were started on metformin 1000 mg/day. If, at 1 month, fasting plasma glucose (FPG) concentration was > 6.1 mmol/l (110 mg/dl), metformin was increased to 2000 mg and glipizide was added at 5 mg/day. If, at 2 months, FPG was > 6.1 mmol/l (110 mg/dl) or HbA1c was > 6.5% (48 mmol/mol), glipizide was increased to 10 mg/day and then to 20 mg/day. If, at 3 months, FPG was > 6.1 mmol/l (110 mg/dl) or HbA1c > 6.5% (48 mmol/mol), glargine insulin was started at 10 units before breakfast and escalated weekly by 1–5 units based on the FPG and HbA1c to 60 units/day to maintain FPG <6.1 mmol/l (110 mg/dl). The effect of therapy on glucose control at 6 months is reported to allow the full effect of therapy on the HbA1c to become manifest. Before the start of therapy, subjects received a 2-hour 75-gram OGTT after 10–12 hour overnight fast. Blood samples were drawn before and every 30 minutes after glucose ingestion for the measurement of plasma glucose, insulin, and C-peptide concentrations. Calculations and Statistical Analysis OGTT-derived indices of insulin sensitivity and insulin secretion were calculated from the plasma glucose, insulin and C-peptide concentrations during the OGTT as previously described ( – ). The Matsuda Index ( ) was used to quantitate insulin sensitivity. The incremental area under the plasma glucose, insulin, and C-peptide concentrations during the OGTT was calculated according to the trapezoid rule. Plasma C-peptide concentration during the OGTT was utilized to quantitate insulin secretion. The ratio between the incremental area under the plasma C-peptide concentration curve to incremental area under plasma glucose concentration curve during the OGTT (ΔCPEP/ΔG) 0–120 was used to provide a measure of insulin secretion. Beta cell function was measured by expressing insulin secretion per prevailing level of insulin resistance: (ΔCPEP/ΔG) 0–120 ÷ IR). C-Peptide response during the OGTT was defined as the ratio between the plasma C-Peptide concentration at 120 minutes during the OGTT and the fasting (time zero) plasma C-peptide concentration (CPEP 120 /CPEP 0 ). Assessment of the predictive discrimination of significant independent predictors was made with the receiver-operating characteristic (ROC) curve by plotting the sensitivity against the corresponding false-positive rate ( ). The area under the ROC curve (aROC) was used as a measure of how well a continuous variable predicted the need for insulin therapy. The algorithm of DeLong et al ( ) was utilized to test significant differences between ROC areas of different parameters. The optimal cut point value of predictor for identifying responders to therapy was determined with the Youden index [maximum sum of sensitivity plus specificity] which maximizes the vertical distance from the line of equality to identify the point on the curve farthest from chance ( ). To assess the predictive power of baseline characteristics in identifying subjects who require insulin therapy we created a multivariate regression model with the need for insulin therapy as the dependent variable and age, gender, BMI, disease duration, HbA1c, FPG, FPI, systolic blood pressure and triglycerides concentration as independent variable. The aROC under the probabilities of the multivariate logistic model was used to compare the predictive discrimination of the model with other prediction parameters. Values are presented as mean ± standard error of mean (SEM). Analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to compare mean differences amongst groups. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05. Bonferroni correction was utilized to correct for multiple comparisons when applicable. DISCUSSION The major finding of the present study is that the majority, approximately two thirds, of newly diagnosed, drug naïve T2DM patients with HbA1c >10% and symptoms of hyperglycemia, e.g. weight loss, achieved good glycemic control (~7.0%) within a short period of ~3 months, and tight glycemic control (<6.5%) within 6 months without the need for insulin therapy. Of note, the percentage of patients achieving the treatment goal was statistically similar between the two treatment groups. This emphasizes that more than one non-insulin therapy is available for newly diagnosed T2DM patients with HbA1c >10%, and insulin is not the only effective glucose lowering therapy in this patient population. Assessing insulin secretion with CPEP120/CPEP0 can guide the decision about the need of insulin administration at the time of T2DM diagnosis. Initiation of insulin therapy is the recommended therapeutic option in subjects with new onset diabetes and HbA1C >10%. ( , ), followed by a switch to non-insulin therapy after HbA1c reduction to the treatment target. In the present study, 78% of subjects receiving initial Triple Therapy and 61% of subjects receiving Conventional Therapy achieved excellent glycemic control (HbA1c <6.5%) within 6 months without the need for insulin therapy. Because study participants were newly diagnosed, relatively young, and free of diabetes complications, a stringent target of glycemic control (HbA1c <6.5%) was utilize in the present study. It is likely that using a higher HbA1c treatment goal (<7.0%) would have resulted in smaller number of subjects requiring insulin therapy. These results are consistent with our previous studies in which combination therapy with a GLP-1 RA plus pioglitazone produced optimal glycemic control in the majority (~80%) of poorly controlled T2DM with long standing disease and HbA1c>10% on maximum doses of metformin plus sulfonylurea ( , ). Collectively, the results demonstrate the presence of non-insulin therapeutic options other than insulin in patients with HbA1c >10%. The second important finding of the present study is that, regardless of the treatment assignment, achievement of the treatment goal (HbA1c <6.5%) without the need for insulin was highly dependent upon the insulin secretory response to the glucose load (OGTT). Subjects in both treatment groups who achieved HbA1c <6.5% without insulin had greater beta cell function, measured with the disposition index, compared to their counterparts who required insulin for glucose control (2.56 and 2.61 folds for subjects receiving Triple Therapy and Conventional Therapy, respectively) ( , ). This finding emphasizes the heterogeneity of T2DM with regard to the disease pathophysiology ( ), and demonstrates that the severe beta cell dysfunction (insulin deficient) phenotype is evident in approximately one-third of T2DM patients with HbA1c >10% at the time of diagnosis. From the clinical standpoint, this subgroup of newly diagnosed T2DM will require long term insulin replacement therapy for optimal glycemic control. Because early metabolic control in T2DM is essential for the prevention of diabetic microvascular complications ( – ), it is important to identify this large subgroup of patients at the time of diabetes diagnosis and appropriately administer insulin therapy to achieve the treatment goal of glucose control in order to reduce their risk for diabetic vascular complications. The increase in plasma C-peptide concentration at 120 minutes after glucose ingestion over baseline was the strongest predictor of metformin- or metformin/sulfonylurea-treated subjects who required insulin therapy. In the Conventional Therapy arm a CPEP120/CPEP0 cut point of > 1.7 identified subjects who required insulin therapy with 91% sensitivity and 42% specificity versus those who achieved the treatment target (HbA1c <6.5%) without insulin. Since metformin is the first line therapy recommended by all guidelines ( , ), this cut point of CPEP 120 /CPEP 0 provides a useful clinical tool to identify newly diagnosed T2DM patients with initial HbA1c >10% who will require long term insulin therapy versus those who will achieve the treatment goal without insulin therapy. Surprisingly, insulin resistance measured with the Matsuda index was comparable amongst subjects requiring insulin therapy and those who achieved the glucose control without insulin in both treatment groups. Further, the Matsuda index was a poor predictor of which subjects required insulin therapy. Because the majority of the study participants were obese or morbidly obese, and the mean BMI did not differ between subjects who required insulin and those who did not (35.5±1.1 vs 35.3±1.1, respectively, p=ns), both groups manifested severe insulin resistance and therefore, insulin resistance did not distinguish between those who require insulin from those who did not. In subjects receiving initial Triple Therapy (but not in the Conventional Therapy group), the FPG concentration and age played a role in identifying which patients would require insulin in subjects with CPEP 120 /CPEP 0 <1.7. All subjects (Triple and Conventional Therapy groups) with CPEP 120 /CPEP 0 >1.7 achieved the treatment goal of HbA1c <6.5% independent of their FPG concentration or HbA1c. On the other hand, ~one third of subjects with CPEP 120 /CPEP 0 <1.7 plus FPG >269 mg/dl (14.9 mmol/l) in the Triple Therapy group required insulin. Age also was significant predictor of need for insulin therapy with tendency of younger patients to require insulin administration. However, adding age and other baseline characteristics to FPG concentration did not improve its predictive power. This observation suggests that despites the advanced beta cell failure in this group of patients (i.e. with HbA1c >10%), Triple Therapy, unlike Conventional Therapy, is capable of improving beta cell function in many patients (e.g. with FPG <269 mg/dl, [14.9 mmol/l]), and reduces the HbA1c to the treatment goal. This can be explained by the strong effect of pioglitazone and GLP-1 RA to directly improve beta cell function independent of lowering the plasma glucose concentration ( – ). Thus, wider population with different characteristics responded to Triple Therapy than to Conventional Therapy. Thus, if Triple Therapy was the treatment of choice in newly diagnosed T2DM patients with HbA1c >10%, only subjects with CPEP 120 /CPEP 0 <1.7 and FPG concentration >269 mg/dl, (14.9 mmol/l), should be considered for addition of basal insulin ( ). The present study has some limitations. It was a post hoc analysis in a single center study. Thus, the number of patients was relatively small (n=104) and primarily of Mexican American ethnicity. Thus, a larger, prospective multicenter multiethnic study is warranted to confirm the generalizability of the present study results. In summary, the CPEP 120 /CPEP 0 ratio of 1.7 provides a useful clinical tool to individualize glucose lowering therapy in newly diagnosed T2DM patients with HbA1c >10% ( ). Subjects with CPEP 120 /CPEP 0 >1.7 are unlikely to require insulin for glucose control, whether they are started on Triple Therapy or Conventional Therapy. Subjects with CPEP 120 /CPEP 0 <1.7 who are started on metformin monotherapy or metformin plus sulfonylurea (Conventional Therapy) are likely to require insulin. If the CPEP 120 /CPEP 0 < 1.7 and the FPG concentration is >269 mg/dl, (14.9 mmol/l), even subjects started on Triple Therapy are likely to require insulin.
